definition: In developmental psychology, a phrase can mean a short spoken expression used in caregiver-child communication, such as common statements parents say in everyday situations. Research on parenting phrases examines how these recurring verbal messages relate to dimensions of parenting like warmth and control.

reasons: The packet supports a specific research topic about “parenting phrases” in caregiver-child communication, not the general dictionary sense of the term “phrase” in developmental psychology.
The definition’s opening claim that a phrase “can mean a short spoken expression” is too broad and not established by the packet as the intended sense.

The wording “such as common statements parents say in everyday situations” is only partly supported; the source discusses frequently used parenting phrases, but not a general definitional sense for phrases overall.
The packet does not support redefining the general term “phrase” as a caregiver-child communication unit; it specifically studies “parenting phrases” used in caregiver-child situations.
The packet frames the work as investigating “phrases frequently used in parenting situations,” rather than providing a general definition of “phrase” in developmental psychology.

The second sentence claims research relates parenting phrases to warmth and control, but the packet only states they were contextualized within warmth/control research dimensions; it also reports that parental warmth and control were not significantly associated with self-esteem, so the “relate to dimensions” wording is not well-supported as a finding.
